subject: Heat Transfer
summary: black and grey bodies (Stefan–Boltzmann, Wien, Kirchhoff), shape factors (reciprocity, summation, crossed strings), the radiation network, parallel plates and radiation shields, and heat exchangers by the LMTD and ε–NTU methods

questions.text: If the absolute temperature of a black body is doubled, its total emissive power becomes
solution: Concept: Stefan–Boltzmann law: Eb = σT⁴.
Eb ∝ T⁴, so doubling T gives 2⁴ = 16 times the emissive power.
Wien's law also says the peak shifts to half the wavelength.
Exam tip: Always use kelvin: doubling 300 °C is not doubling the absolute temperature.

questions.text: A grey surface of emissivity 0.7 is at 600 °C. Taking σ = 5.67 × 10<sup>−8</sup> W/m²·K⁴, its total emissive power (in kW/m², round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: For a grey surface E = εσT⁴ with T in kelvin.
Exam tip: Using T = 873 K instead of 873.15 K changes the answer only in the third significant figure; using °C gives nonsense.

questions.text: For an opaque grey surface, the correct relation between absorptivity α, reflectivity ρ and emissivity ε is
solution: Concept: Radiation falling on a surface is absorbed, reflected or transmitted: α + ρ + τ = 1.
Opaque: τ = 0, so α + ρ = 1.
Grey (Kirchhoff): ε = α, hence ε = 1 − ρ.
Exam tip: A polished metal (high ρ) is therefore a poor emitter: that is why radiation shields are polished.

questions.text: A small sphere of 0.2 m diameter is placed inside a closed cubical box of side 0.5 m. The shape factor from the inner surface of the box to the sphere (round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: The sphere (1) is convex and enclosed, so F12 = 1. Reciprocity: A1F12 = A2F21.
Exam tip: The rest of the box's radiation, F22 = 0.916, falls back on the box itself.

questions.text: Two long parallel plates of equal width w face each other directly at a separation h = w, as shown. By the crossed-strings method, the shape factor between them is
solution: Concept: Hottel's crossed strings for long surfaces: F12 = (sum of crossed strings − sum of uncrossed strings)/(2 × width of surface 1).
Crossed strings (diagonals): 2√(w² + h²) = 2√2 w; uncrossed strings (the open sides): 2h = 2w
Exam tip: As h/w → 0 the plates become 'infinite' and F12 → 1.

questions.text: Two very large parallel plates are at 1000 K (ε = 0.9) and 400 K (ε = 0.5). Taking σ = 5.67 × 10<sup>−8</sup> W/m²·K⁴, the net radiation heat flux between them (in kW/m², round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Two-surface enclosure of large parallel plates: q = σ(T1⁴ − T2⁴)/(1/ε1 + 1/ε2 − 1).
Exam tip: The surface with the lower emissivity controls the exchange: raising ε2 to 0.9 would give 45.2 kW/m².

questions.text: The radiation network between two surfaces 1 and 2 of an enclosure consists of, in series,
opts: two space resistances and one surface resistance
solution: Concept: Each surface has a surface resistance (1 − ε)/(εA) between Eb and its radiosity J.
Between the two radiosities lies the space (geometric) resistance 1/(A<sub>1</sub>F<sub>12</sub>).
q<sub>12</sub> = (E<sub>b1</sub> − E<sub>b2</sub>)/[(1 − ε<sub>1</sub>)/(ε<sub>1</sub>A<sub>1</sub>) + 1/(A<sub>1</sub>F<sub>12</sub>) + (1 − ε<sub>2</sub>)/(ε<sub>2</sub>A<sub>2</sub>)].
Exam tip: For a black surface (ε = 1) the surface resistance vanishes and J = Eb.

questions.text: Radiation shields, all with the same emissivity as the two large parallel plates between which they are placed, are used to cut the radiation heat transfer to less than 15 % of its unshielded value. The minimum number of shields needed is ______
solution: Concept: With n shields of the same emissivity, there are n + 1 equal resistances in series, so qn/q0 = 1/(n + 1).
Minimum n = 6 (q falls to 1/7 = 14.3 %)
Exam tip: Five shields give 1/6 = 16.7 %, just short: check the boundary case.

questions.text: In a steam condenser, the steam condenses at constant temperature while cooling water flows through the tubes. For given inlet and outlet temperatures, the LMTD for counter-flow compared with parallel-flow is
solution: Concept: When one fluid stays at a constant temperature, the terminal temperature differences ΔT1 and ΔT2 are the same whichever way the other fluid flows.
Hence the LMTD and the required area are the same for counter-flow and parallel-flow.
Likewise C<sub>r</sub> = 0 and ε = 1 − e<sup>−NTU</sup> for every arrangement.
Exam tip: Without phase change, counter-flow always gives the larger LMTD.

questions.text: In a parallel-flow heat exchanger, the hot fluid cools from 180 °C to 120 °C and the cold fluid is heated from 30 °C to 90 °C. The LMTD (in °C, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: LMTD = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2), with the ΔT at each end of the exchanger.
Parallel flow: inlet end ΔT<sub>1</sub> = 180 − 30 = 150 °C; outlet end ΔT<sub>2</sub> = 120 − 90 = 30 °C
Exam tip: In counter-flow the same terminal temperatures would give ΔT = 90 °C at both ends, so LMTD = 90 °C.

questions.text: Oil and water have the same heat capacity rate, 5 kW/K, in a counter-flow heat exchanger. Oil enters at 140 °C; water enters at 40 °C and leaves at 100 °C. With U = 500 W/m²·K, the required heat transfer area (in m²) is ______
solution: Concept: For balanced counter-flow (Ch = Cc), the temperature difference is the same all along the exchanger, so LMTD = ΔT.
Exam tip: The LMTD formula gives 0/0 here; recognise the parallel lines instead.

questions.text: The number of transfer units (NTU) of a heat exchanger is defined as
solution: Concept: NTU = UA/Cmin, a measure of the exchanger's thermal size.
Option (B) is the capacity ratio C<sub>r</sub>; option (D) is the effectiveness ε.
ε = f(NTU, C<sub>r</sub>, flow arrangement).
Exam tip: Use the ε–NTU method when outlet temperatures are unknown; LMTD then needs trial and error.

questions.text: In a parallel-flow heat exchanger, NTU = 1.5 and C<sub>r</sub> = 0.5, with C<sub>min</sub> = 3 kW/K. The hot fluid enters at 130 °C and the cold fluid at 30 °C. Using ε = [1 − exp(−NTU(1 + C<sub>r</sub>))]/(1 + C<sub>r</sub>), the heat transfer rate (in kW, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Q = εQmax, with Qmax = Cmin(Th,i − Tc,i).
Exam tip: A parallel-flow exchanger can never exceed ε = 1/(1 + Cr) = 0.667 here, however large it is.

questions.text: The maximum possible heat transfer rate in a heat exchanger is
solution: Concept: The largest temperature change any fluid can undergo is Th,i − Tc,i.
Only the fluid with the smaller heat capacity rate can actually achieve it (in an infinitely long counter-flow exchanger).
So Qmax = Cmin(Th,i − Tc,i); using Cmax would violate the energy balance of the other fluid.
Exam tip: ε = Q/Qmax lies between 0 and 1 by this definition.

questions.text: The radiosity of a surface is
opts: the radiation emitted by the surface per unit area
the radiation incident on the surface per unit area
the radiation absorbed by the surface per unit area
the total radiation leaving the surface (emitted plus reflected) per unit area
questions.ans: (D) the total radiation leaving the surface (emitted plus reflected) per unit area
solution: Concept: Radiosity J = εEb + ρG, where G is the irradiation (incident radiation).
It is everything leaving the surface: emitted and reflected.
Option (B) is the irradiation G.
Exam tip: Net radiation from an opaque surface = A(J − G) = (Eb − J)/[(1 − ε)/(εA)].
